survey: A western saddle shown in three-quarter side view, straddling a wooden fence rail. The rail runs left to right, through the gullet from front to back. The rail runs off both edges of the frame, so its posts are simply out of view. The horn sits on a short neck at the front (left) end. The dished seat curves up into a raised cantle at the back (right). The seat sits on top of the skirts, and its underside rests on the top of the rail. The near skirt hangs down in front of the rail. The far skirt shows behind the rail at the right, so the rail correctly runs between the two skirts. The near stirrup leather comes down from under the seat roll, over the skirt, through a metal buckle, and holds the near stirrup. The far stirrup hangs behind it, slightly offset. Its leather is hidden by the near skirt, which is what you would expect, since it hangs from the far side of the saddle. Both stirrups are the same symmetric arch with a flat tread. There is no cinch or rigging, but that is an acceptable simplification for a saddle stored on a rail. Every part attaches where it should, the saddle rests on the rail rather than floating, the parts are counted correctly (one horn, one cantle, two skirts, two stirrups), and it could do its job.
